title: Is Electrostatic Disinfection Spraying Included in Standard Cleaning or Billed Extra?
seoTitle: Is Electrostatic Disinfection Included in Office Cleaning Quotes?
metaDescription: Find out when electrostatic disinfection spraying is included in monthly janitorial retainers vs billed at $0.05–$0.18/sq ft. Audit quotes with our tool.
excerpt: Most commercial janitorial contracts include manual touchpoint wiping in their base monthly retainer but exclude full-suite electrostatic disinfection spraying. Learn how to audit your scope of work to distinguish baseline EPA List N sanitizing from billable electrostatic work orders.
quickAnswer: In standard US commercial office janitorial contracts ($0.05 to $0.20 per sq ft per visit), manual microfiber wiping of high-touch surfaces (door hardware, restroom fixtures, breakroom counters) is included in the base monthly retainer, whereas full-suite electrostatic disinfection spraying is almost always billed as an extra add-on ($0.04 to $0.15 per sq ft per pass, or $55 to $95 per specialty technician hour, subject to a $125 to $250 trip minimum). Only high-frequency 5x/week medical-adjacent or large 25,000+ sq ft contracts occasionally bundle weekly common-area electrostatic misting into the base fee.

blocks.text: The Contract Divide: Manual Touchpoint Disinfection vs. Electrostatic Spraying

One of the most frequent invoicing disputes between corporate facility managers and commercial cleaning contractors erupts during winter respiratory illness spikes. An office manager assumes that because their monthly janitorial agreement specifies 'nightly disinfection of restrooms, breakrooms, and high-touch office surfaces,' the crew is already applying broad-spectrum electrostatic misting across workstations. When an employee reports a confirmed norovirus, influenza, or COVID-19 exposure and the property manager requests an immediate suite-wide electrostatic treatment, the vendor submits an extra-service work order for $350 to $1,800.

Why is there an extra charge for electrostatic disinfection spraying when disinfection is already written into the contract? The distinction comes down to application mechanics, chemical consumption, EPA dwell-time labor, and capital equipment amortization. Standard nightly cleaning relies on the two-step spray-and-wipe method using color-coded microfiber cloths on a defined list of 15 to 25 high-touch points per zone. Electrostatic spraying uses a specialized positive-charge atomizing nozzle (typically 40 to 110 microns) to wrap cationic disinfectant droplets 360 degrees around complex three-dimensional geometries—chair armrests, keyboard undersides, partition fabrics, and locker pulls—that manual wiping cannot cover at standard ISSA production speeds of 3,500 square feet per hour.

blocks.text: Why Vendors Exclude Electrostatic Spraying from Base Per-Square-Foot Retainers

When a janitorial contractor bids a 12,000-square-foot office suite at a 3x-week frequency (13.0 visits per month, using the standard 4.33 weeks-per-month multiplier and a 0.95 frequency factor), the base rate sits between $0.07 and $0.12 per square foot per visit. That price is engineered around rapid workflow: one technician empties trash and dust-mops hard surfaces, another runs a commercial HEPA backpack vacuum across carpet tiles (1.0x flooring multiplier), and a third sanitizes the restrooms and breakroom.

Electrostatic disinfection cannot legally or scientifically replace that baseline cleaning pass. Every EPA-registered hospital and commercial disinfectant label explicitly states that surfaces must be pre-cleaned of visible organic soil, dust, and grease before applying electrostatic mist. If a technician sprays electrostatically charged hypochlorous acid or hydrogen peroxide over a dusty desk or a coffee-stained conference table without pre-wiping, the biofilm shields pathogens and leaves a sticky residue on computer monitors. Consequently, electrostatic spraying is pure additive labor and chemical expense on top of the baseline clean.

blocks.title: Beware of 'Free' Electrostatic Spraying Claims in Low-Bid Proposals
blocks.text: If a competing bidder promises '100% free nightly electrostatic spraying across your entire office' inside a rock-bottom $0.06/sq ft quote, audit their chemical budget and labor hours immediately. In practice, dishonest operators either skip the mandatory manual pre-wipe, dilute quaternary disinfectants below EPA-required ppm thresholds, or only mist the restrooms for 90 seconds while logging the whole floor.
Three Contract Models: How Facility Managers Structure Electrostatic Pricing

Rather than waiting for an outbreak to negotiate emergency rates under duress, seasoned procurement teams structure electrostatic disinfection into their Master Services Agreement (MSA) using one of three transparent billing architectures:

items: Model 1: High-Density Zone Bundling (Common Areas Only): For offices on a 5x-week daily schedule (21.65 visits/month, 0.90 frequency multiplier), the vendor includes a Friday night electrostatic pass strictly for high-density zones—restrooms, breakrooms, fitness rooms, and conference rooms—adding just $75 to $185 per month to the base retainer.

Model 2: Pre-Negotiated Per-Square-Foot Rate Card (On-Call Rider): The base contract covers standard manual disinfection, while Schedule B locks in a pre-negotiated add-on rate of $0.05 to $0.09 per square foot (or $65/hr specialty labor with a $135 minimum visit charge matching standard trip minimums) whenever HR triggers a post-exposure clean.

Model 3: Seasonal Flu-Window Escalator (November through March): The facility pays the standard baseline retainer for seven months of the year, then automatically activates a weekly or biweekly (2.17 visits/month) electrostatic application across open-plan workstations during peak winter viral transmission months.

blocks.text: Pre-Cleaning Logistics & Cross-Contamination Hardware Required Before Spraying

Whether you negotiate electrostatic misting as a weekly bundled tier or a per-incident work order, your contract specifications should mandate strict pre-cleaning hardware to protect sensitive office electronics and prevent cross-contamination between zones. Because electrostatic droplets carry a positive charge that seeks grounded surfaces, any loose litter, paper scraps, or surface grime left behind will be encapsulated in wet chemical film.

Professional crews stage their pre-spray workflow using a dedicated mobile supply platform such as the Rubbermaid Commercial Utility Service Cart 3-Shelf (rated for a 500-pound capacity across three structural foam shelves with 4-inch non-marking casters), allowing technicians to transport bulk EPA List N disinfectant gallons, paper restocks, and sprayer batteries in a single pass. Before energizing the electrostatic nozzle, crews clear exterior entry aprons and floor litter using an ergonomic Unger Nifty Nabber 36-Inch Commercial Trash Picker Grabber (steel claws with a 10-pound lift rating) and execute manual surface pre-wiping with Microfiber Wholesale 16x16 Commercial Cleaning Cloths (150-Pack, 300 GSM 4-color OSHA cross-contamination coding: red for restroom fixtures, yellow for vanity and glass partitions, green for breakroom counters, and blue for general desk surfaces).
How to Audit an Electrostatic Disinfection Quote in 4 Steps
Before signing an annual janitorial agreement or approving an extra-charge disinfection invoice, run the vendor's proposal through this four-step contract audit checklist:

items.name: Step 1: Verify the EPA Registration Number and Wet Dwell Time
items.text: Demand the exact EPA Registration Number and Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for the electrostatic solution. Prefer 1-to-3-minute contact time oxidizing agents (hypochlorous acid or accelerated hydrogen peroxide) over 10-minute sticky quaternary ammonium compounds that leave residue on keyboards.

items.name: Step 2: Separate Pre-Cleaning Labor from Spraying Production Rates
items.text: Confirm that your nightly retainer already covers the manual soil pre-wipe. A technician with a backpack electrostatic sprayer covers 10,000 to 15,000 sq ft per hour during the misting pass itself; never pay standard slow-wipe labor hours twice.

items.name: Step 3: Check Minimum Trip Charges Against Scheduled Visit Days
items.text: If you schedule electrostatic spraying on a night when the janitorial crew is already on-site (e.g., Wednesday or Friday evening), require the vendor to waive the standalone $90–$135 minimum trip charge and bill strictly for the incremental 45–90 minutes of specialty spraying.

items.name: Step 4: Define Sensitive Equipment Masking & Paper Handling Rules
items.text: Ensure the scope specifies micron particle size (40–80 microns) and distance protocols (3 to 6 feet from monitors and open paper files) so electrostatic mist sanitizes touchpoints without saturating sensitive IT hardware.

faqs.q: Why can't electrostatic spraying replace our regular nightly desk and restroom wiping?
faqs.a: EPA disinfectant registration laws require surfaces to be free of visible organic soil before chemical disinfection can achieve its stated log-kill claim. Electrostatic sprayers apply a fine chemical mist without mechanical friction; they cannot remove coffee rings, skin oils, dust, or restroom soil without a prior microfiber wipe using color-coded 300 GSM cloths.

faqs.q: What is a fair per-square-foot price for add-on electrostatic disinfection in a 10,000 sq ft office?
faqs.a: When added onto an existing nightly cleaning visit where the crew is already on-site and pre-cleaning is complete, electrostatic spraying typically costs $0.04 to $0.08 per square foot ($400 to $800 for a 10,000 sq ft floor). If ordered as an emergency standalone weekend dispatch after a confirmed illness exposure, rates rise to $0.09 to $0.16 per square foot to cover mobilization and specialty labor ($55–$95/hr).

faqs.q: Does OSHA require special hazard communication or ventilation delays when vendors use electrostatic sprayers?
faqs.a: Yes. Under OSHA HazCom (29 CFR 1910.1200), the contractor must maintain an accessible Safety Data Sheet (SDS) on-site, equip the spraying technician with eye protection and respiratory PPE matching the chemical SDS, and perform spraying when office occupants are absent, adhering to the product's reentry interval (typically 15 to 30 minutes after mist settling).

faqs.q: How does the 4.33 weeks-per-month formula affect weekly electrostatic add-on billing?
faqs.a: Because a calendar year has 52 weeks across 12 months, a weekly (1x/week) electrostatic pass equals 4.33 visits per month—not 4.0. If a vendor quotes $150 per weekly electrostatic pass, your fixed monthly amortized invoice should be $649.50 ($150 x 4.33), ensuring four-week and five-week months are billed uniformly.
